subsubtopic: SUGGESTED IMPLEMENTATION OF RECOMMENDATIONS OF TARIFF BOARD REPORT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under Standing Order 43. My motion is prompted by the failure of this government in protecting the livelihoods of Canadian farmers, thus endangering our nation's future food supply. In light of the fact that excessive agricultural imports have, under this administration, now needlessly jeopardized farm producers' futures, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes):
That this House directs the government to bring forward immediate measures to implement those recommendations of the Tariff Board report which bring Canadian tariffs on agricultural products into line with those of our competitors.

subsubtopic: CONDEMNATION OF DISCRIMINATION IN PROVISION FOR ENTITLEMENT TO BENEFITS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43, which arises from the changes announced in the unemployment insurance legislation that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration brought before the committee yesterday. The motion is as follows:
That this House condemns the Minister of Manpower and Immigration for introducing changes in the unemployment insurance legislation which for the first time in Canadian history discriminate among Canadian workers, entitling some to collect benefits after a shorter period of attachment to the labour force than others, although all Canadian workers pay precisely the same premiums.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATING IN INTERNATIONAL COMPETITION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of recent unsportsmanlike protests made in this House and across Canada aimed at Team Canada's performance in Vienna, and even with all this skepticism Team Canada, playing under unfamiliar conditions and regulations, managed a comeback yesterday by tying the current world hockey champions-I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will allow me to move, based on the fact that a negative motion dealing with this same subject matter was allowed to be put just two days ago, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski):
That this House give our young hockey ambassadors abroad the encouragement they deserve by congratulating them for their comeback game yesterday and wishing them all the best for the remaining part of the series.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATING IN INTERNATIONAL COMPETITION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: PARTICIPATING IN INTERNATIONAL COMPETITION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext: Order, please. I do not wish to be unduly restrictive, but one of the concerns I have had in messages of congratulation, pursuant to Standing Order 43, relates to those directed toward communities. With regard to one which was put yesterday, I am sure the House have noticed that I did not put the question. The motions that were put previously did have, aside from the congratulatory message, some connection with the administration of Hockey Canada which has, at least, a connection with the administrative responsibilities of the government. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask the unanimous consent of the House to deal with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that the amendment to Bill C-27, announced by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration regarding minor attachments is expressly discriminatory against the vast numbers of unemployed in Canada, and since the Canadian Bill of Rights specifically prohibits discrimination within a class of persons or between classes of persons, and in view of the fact that this proposed amendment pits unemployed against unemployed, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Sault Ste. speechtext:

subsubtopic: REASON CHEESE IMPORTS ARE NOT REDUCED

In view of the fact that the United States legislation provides for an additional 90 days for the President to delay his decision in terms of the Alaska gas to the U.S. Congress, has the Prime Minister requested the President to extend his own time frame in terms of that decision-making which he is allowed to do, in order to give Canadian agencies a full opportunity to examine the many difficult questions surrounding that decision?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: NATURAL GAS-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF TIME FOR DECISION ON CONSTRUCTION OF PIPELINE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the 90 day extension is well known to the President and myself. He is obviously aiming for the earliest possible date. The only commitment I gave to him was that we would undertake to get a statement of Canadian views to him at the earliest possible moment, hopefully before late September. If we cannot get our opinions to him by then, he will have to make up his mind. The hon. member realizes he might use his extra 90 days or he may announce a decision regardless of what may be in the Canadian interest. That is why it is in our interest to get this decision as soon as possible. The hon. member knows that the National Energy Board, and indeed the Berger commission, are taking much longer than they had hoped. They are doing a very difficult task. We understand that. However, there cannot be any added delays if we want to make a decision within a time which would be useful to the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: CONFLICT BETWEEN MINISTERS ON VALUE OF MARKETING BOARDS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Recent statements by the Minister of Agriculture point to the fact that he feels marketing boards as currently set up are virtually sacrosanct. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has made repeated statements contradicting the minister. He has brought a bill before this House which will practically outlaw them. Will the Prime Minister now blow his Prime Ministerial referee's whistle and tell us which minister is actually speaking for the government?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: CONFLICT BETWEEN MINISTERS ON VALUE OF MARKETING BOARDS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no contradiction. If the hon. member will give me a moment, I will explain. The government believes in marketing boards, but it does not believe that marketing boards are the answer to every agricultural problem. That is why the Minister of Agriculture, with cabinet authority and parliamentary authority, has set up some marketing boards which are for the good of the consumer and the good of the producer. We support that. This does not mean that every agricultural problem calls for a solution by way of a marketing board.
The wheat stabilization act, for instance, brings in another concept, one of income stabilization rather than supply management. That is why there is complete support in cabinet for the position of the Minister of Agriculture. It does not mean that there will be marketing boards everywhere. It means that if they are necessary, desirable and useful they will be brought in. We know that among the cattlemen, for instance, there is opposition to the concept of marketing boards and there is no indication that we are going to force any on them.
So far as the bill before the House is concerned, the hon. member will have a chance to speak to it in committee. It is not the intent of the bill to destroy or to attack marketing boards. If clarification is called for it will be brought in at the time of debate in committee.

subsubtopic: CONFLICT BETWEEN MINISTERS ON VALUE OF MARKETING BOARDS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. It is not only a question of the bill brought forward but of the
Oral Questions
declarations of the minister and a report that was brought out by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Is it the position of the right hon. Prime Minister that in the area of food marketing boards two ministers of his cabinet can make at this stage diametrically opposed declarations on the subject and get away with it in terms of clarification in the minds of the opposition and the public?

subsubtopic: CONFLICT BETWEEN MINISTERS ON VALUE OF MARKETING BOARDS-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I repeat part of my answer. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has expressed the view, which is also that of cabinet, that marketing boards, in other words supply management, should not apply to every agricultural problem. I gave as an example a government act which does not use this approach. Therefore, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is perfectly justified in saying he does not believe that marketing boards are the answer to everything.

subsubtopic: INABILITY OF TOBACCO FARMERS TO OBTAIN CARIBBEAN WORKERS-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is appropriate in times of high unemployment that requests for Caribbean and Mexican workers are approved only if Canadians cannot be identified by the department as available for the job. The problem that we have is perhaps more of a human one than a legislative one, namely that when individuals are referred to jobs, some stay an hour, some stay a week. Do they have bona fide reasons for leaving, or are job conditions poor, or is the pay poor? As I say, it is really more of a human problem than one regarding which we can legislate.
Our responsibility as those who should be looking after unemployed Canadians is that they be given the first opportunity to work at these jobs. The reports that I am receiving, unhappily, from both sides of the House are, quite candidly, that Canadians are going in but are not sticking with the job,

April 27, 1977
Oral Questions
for what they feel are quite legitimate reasons. The employer does not think that they are. I do not wish to flood the market, as it were, with Caribbean and Mexican workers at a time of high unemployment, but the situation seems to be that we may have to look with a little less jaundiced eye in that direction.

speechtext: Do you want to know my strategy?

speechtext: Ho, ho!

subsubtopic: LONG-TERM EFFECTS OF WATER FLUORIDATION
speechtext:
1.	To the knowledge of the government, has the Federal Drug Administration in the United States announced its intention to research the long-term health effects of water fluoridation and, if so, is the government co-operating with the FDA to keep abreast of American research developments in this area of public health?
2.	Is the government aware of the research Findings of the noted biologist, Dr. Edward Groth III of the California Institute of Technology in the area of water fluoridation and, if so, is the government aware of Dr. Groth's recommendation to the FDA that research into the long-term effects of water fluoridation is needed?
3.	Is the government monitoring on a nation-wide basis the possible long-term public health side effects of water fluoridation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: LONG-TERM EFFECTS OF WATER FLUORIDATION
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of National Health and Welfare is concerned: 1. To the knowledge of the government, the federal food and drug administration in the United States has not announced any intention to undertake new research on the long-term effects of water fluoridation; responsibility for coordination and advice on water fluoridation programmes in the United States lies with other units of the Public Health Service. Research on the long-term health effects of environmental chemicals, which is undertaken by various United States government agencies, is co-ordinated by the Committee for the Co-ordination of Toxicology and Related Programmes, to which the Health Protection Branch is invited to send an observer. This assures that the Canadian government keeps abreast of all United States government research developments in this area of public health.
2.	In 1974, Dr. Edward Groth III sent his Ph.D dissertation to the United States food and drug administration. In the opinion of scientists of the food and drug administration, work reported in the thesis was essentially uncritical, biased and not supportive of public health practices. Scientists of the Health Protection Branch have not reviewed Dr. Groth's Ph.D dissertation.
3.	A retrospective epidemiology study in selected Canadian cities where municipal water supplies are fluoridated is in progress at the present time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE THE MAXIMUM LIABILITY OF THE CORPORATION AND CREDIT GUARANTEES
speechtext:
that Bill C-47, to amend the Export Development Act, be read for the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-47 is to amend the Export Development Act by increasing the maximum liability of the Export Development Corporation under insurance contracts as well as the export credit gurantees. This amendment to section 26 of the act would increase the maximum liability for insurance contracts entered into by EDC from $750 million to $2.5 billion. The amendment to section 28 would increase the maximum liability for insurance contracts entered into by the government from $750 million to $1 billion.
The Export Development Corporation provides three major services, namely, export credit insurance and guarantees, long term loans on the purchase of Canadian durable goods and services, and guarantees against political risks for Canadians investing abroad.
The legislation now before us deals only with export credit insurance ceilings. It should be noted that the new maximum liabilities are for eventual liabilities only, rather than direct liabilities as is the case for the loans program. It can therefore be said in confidence that these new limits will not increase funding needs. Because as far as the insurance contracts entered into by the EDC are concerned, revenues derived from premiums have always covered net claims in the past. It should also be noted that insurance contracts and guarantees mainly cover loans from commercial sources.
Recently, requests for export credit insurance from Canadian exporters have reached an unprecedented level. This is not a Canadian phenomenon, because the same problem arises in every major industrialized nation. Due to rising trade, a better knowledge of the EDC programs as well as uncertainty and hard competition in international trade, exporter use of credit insurance has been increasing. This gave rise to greater demand for certain types of insurance. There has been for instance a strong demand for pre-shipping insurance for durable goods projects, a number of which are financed through long term EDC loans. Because the corporation's loans afford no protection during the pre-shipment period, exporters look to an insurance program for a hedge against the numerous losses they may suffer before receiving the proceeds of a loan.
The result of the foregoing is that the present statutory limit for insurance and guarantees is virtually exhausted and EDC cannot now meet the full requirements of Canadian exporters.
April 27, 1977

Furthermore, there are new insurance services in the areas of performance bonds, advance payment guarantees, and consortium cross-liability coverage which EDC will be able to provide as soon as the ceilings are increased. There is a high demand for these new services among exporters who are competing for important turn-key capital goods projects.
During 1976 EDC insured for its own account exports valued at over $1.3 billion. This was an average of over $100 million per month-important business for the Canadian economy. We are now entering the spring shipping season, and the need to keep our exports moving is even more vital.
The ceilings proposed in this bill should be sufficient to accommodate the insurance needs of Canadian exporters through the end of 1978. Well before that time it is intended to place before the House a much more extensive bill dealing with all aspects of the Export Development Corporation.
Hon. members are all aware that success in international trade is absolutely essential to the health of the Canadian economy. Therefore the export credits insurance program of EDC is an important element in facilitating exports. Hence it is in the interest of us all that export business not be lost through the lack of insurance coverage. Therefore I urge an expeditious approval of this bill.
Mir. Jim Balfour (Regina East): Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to oppose or obstruct passage of the bill before us. On the contrary, we on this side have no quarrel with the objects the bill is intended to implement.
Indeed we support this phase of Export Development Corporation activity since in by far the greater number of cases the intervention by it as a guarantor or insurer of foreign financial commitments made to Canadian firms is the only practical method available to make possible a great number of commercial contracts of all kinds negotiated abroad by Canadian firms doing business there.
At the same time, we on this side of the House have serious reservations about the other main activity of the EDC, namely, its activity in the field of direct lending.
As of December 31, 1976, $1.4 billion of public money has been advanced by the Export Development Corporation. I remain far from convinced that the direct lending activities of the EDC constitute the right way to accomplish the object of supporting and encouraging export sales of Canadian manufactured goods abroad. In fact the experience and the methodology of other industrialized countries competing with Canada for export markets suggest it may very well be the wrong way.
I would like to put forward the suggestion this afternoon that the minister and the government re-examine the Canadian approach to export financing, and in particular examine whether this could not better be done by making far greater use of our own private banking industry with the support, where necessary, of the EDC.
I make this suggestion on the following grounds. First, on principle I do not believe that government should directly
Export Development Act
involve itself in commercial activities-and direct loans to foreign buyers of Canadian goods is a commercial activity- except as a lender of last resort.
The system that has developed under current lending practices of the EDC is that conventional banking services are used by the Canadian firm doing business abroad but these services are by-passed and EDC banking services are utilized with respect to loans required offshore in order to complete the financial package necessary to implement the transaction. The result is an unnecessarily cumbersome administrative hodgepodge of financial functions, and because of over-lapping spheres of responsibility inordinate delays occur not infrequently, with the result that the business is lost to a foreign competitor.
How much better it would be if the activities of the EDC could be restructured so that the whole package of financial services required in a particular case could be furnished by the Canadian bank whose customer the Canadian firm happens to be, supported as necessary by EDC guarantees with respect to performance commitments, foreign loan repayments, longterm interest rate stabilization mechanisms, and inflation and exchange risk indemnities, but in the process removing EDC from direct lending activities of public moneys which must necessarily be supplied at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer.
What I suggest is by no means new or unique to other industrial countries. Belgium, Denmark, the Federal Republic of Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and the United States have all established government supported private organizations to offer medium and long-term financing required for doing business in foreign countries.
The Private Export Funding Corporation in the United States provides a unique joint private-government undertaking wherein a consortium of some fifty private banks and industrial companies have provided capital enabling PEFCO to borrow on public markets to fund medium and long-term export credits.
Repayment of the resulting credits is guaranteed by the export-import bank, the counterpart of the EDC, thus giving PEFCO obligations a preferred status in the money market.
Australia, Finland, Greece, Ireland, New Zealand and Spain, have generally followed the pattern of the industrial countries in providing export credit insurance and, more recently, in adding facilities for medium and long-term financing. As the range of exports in any country becomes broader and more diverse, medium and long term financing is required. However, the funding of most medium term financing can be handled satisfactorily by private banking institutions, provided a mechanism is made available by the government to share or assume risk.
I would now like to offer a few more general comments concerning Canada's over-all merchandise trade balance, which I suggest is a cause for concern. This concern is shared, I am sure, by the minister and his colleagues with the hon.

April 27, 1977
Export Development Act
members on this side of the Elouse. Exports and imports of merchandise form the most important part of the receipts and payments on the current account. Our merchandise trade surplus, more or less constant during the 1960's, reached a peak in 1970. It subsequently declined and turned into a deficit toward the end of 1974.
The negative balance in 1975 amounted to $639 million, in balance of payments terms, a figure which represented a decline of $2,337 billion from the preceding year. The 1975 deficit in the merchandise trade balance was caused in part by the world recession, aggravated by numerous strikes domestically and a deterioration in terms of trade abroad.
It is true that our exports showed signs of recovery during 1976 and, indeed, registered a modest surplus of $365 million during the first nine months of last year. It should be noted, however, that this surplus was partly due to a less rapid growth of imports resulting from a stagnation in the level of domestic investment, and also that this improvement in the trade balance was in actual fact relatively modest, if one considers that it occurred during an expansionary period in the world economy, which was particularly evident in the United States, our principal trading partner.
The hard fact is that the deterioration of our foreign trade is not of recent origin. Between 1970 and 1975 Canada's share of world exports fell from 5.9 per cent to 4.2 per cent, and, indeed our current surplus in terms of constant dollars remains slender when compared to those of the late 1960's and at the beginning of the 1970's.
When one examines the data, it is difficult indeed to be optimistic with respect to the medium term outlook for Canada's trade prospects abroad. The various exceptional advances which Canada enjoyed during the 1960's are not likely to re-occur. I refer particularly to the free-trade agreements comparable to the U.S.-Canadian auto pact. Nor is there much likelihood that the spectacular price increases in primary commodities which occurred in 1972 and 1973, to Canada's advantage, will be repeated.
Concern about inflation, caused largely by the simultaneous overheating of the economies of the industrialized nations, has prompted cautious policies on their part which will result in moderating the rate of expansion of their economies.
The increase in energy costs, the tendency toward protectionism becoming more evident in certain countries, and the opposition to uncontrolled growth on behalf of the quality of life will also work in the same direction. The inescapable conclusion is that the expansion of the world economy will be much less pronounced in the next decade than in the last.
In 1975 Canada became a net importer of crude petroleum instead of predominantly an exporter. The federal government has now imposed quotas on petroleum exports to the United States in order to ensure long term supplies for Canada.
Sales to the United States, which reached nearly one million barrels a day in 1974, were limited to 300,000 barrels a day as of last January 1 and will cease entirely by 1982. For a surplus of $761 million in 1974, the trade balance in oil dropped to a

deficit of $972 million during the first 11 months of 1976. Two years from now domestic demand will in all likelihood exceed the productive capacity of Canada, and the deficit on the petroleum account, enlarged by price increases for imported oil, will likely exceed the receipts from exports of natural gas. The exploitation of gas reserves in Arctic regions would be barely adequate to satisfy domestic needs and to honour our export commitments. Consequently, unless new commercially exploitable reserves are discovered, the dependence of Canada on imported petroleum will weigh more and more heavily on the merchandise trade balance.
The outlook for our trade in manufactured products is far from promising. Canada traditionally shows a trade surplus in agriculture commodities, raw materials, and semi-manufactured products but on the other hand, a substantial deficit for its trade in finished products. This deficit has grown worse. It rose from $3.52 billion in 1970 to $10,513 billion in 1975 and to $9,482 billion during the first 11 months of 1976. Even taking higher prices into consideration, the deterioration remains very significant and very ominous.
Trade with the United States in automobiles, parts and accessories, under which Canada enjoyed a surplus in 1970, 1971 and 1972, turned into an adverse balance of $1.7 billion in 1975 and a like figure in 1976, with no evidence of an improving trend.
The performance of Canada in terms of its competitive capacity is another cause for both concern and disappointment when compared with that of the United States, the country which absorbs nearly 70 per cent of our foreign trade. Since 1970 our wages in the manufacturing industry have increased faster than those in the United States and, in addition, the growth rate of our productivity has declined. The result is a weakened competitive position.
A further discouraging development is that of receipts and payments under the heading of services. The deficit position here has likewise grown considerably in recent years, increasing from $1.9 billion in 1970 to $4.3 billion in 1975, and will likely exceed $5 billion in 1976.
During the last ten years Canada has registered only one surplus. That was under the heading of tourism, and that was in 1967, the year of the world exhibition in Montreal.
Under the heading of net payments of interest and dividends, the deficit has greatly increased since 1974, reaching nearly $2 billion in 1975. However, there is a distinct possibility that the net inflow of foreign capital this year may well be inadequate to cover the current account deficit, as in years past. If this were carried to an extreme, the government could find itself with no choice but to commit itself to a restrictive policy, as it did in 1962, in order to correct the size of the current account deficit, a policy which could be disastrous, in regard to current domestic activity, characterized by serious under-utilization of human and material resources.
The deficiency of Canada's industrial structure-in particular of the competitiveness of its manufacturing industry-is the problem which has to be tackled if we want to become
April 27, 1977

something other than exporters of raw materials and importers of capital. The true response to the deterioration of our trade account lies in the expansion of our export of manufactured goods, which is likely to have a direct impact on output and employment.
Fundamental, related issues such as the local processing of our raw materials, the maintenance of sustained economic growth, the creation of jobs, costs and productivity raise questions about the very structure of our economy. In view of the uncertain propects for our balance of payments, it is more pressing than ever to establish the direction of a long term industrial development strategy for Canada, and it is our hope that the minister will undertake this in the very near future.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE THE MAXIMUM LIABILITY OF THE CORPORATION AND CREDIT GUARANTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this certainly is a welcome opportunity to stand and make a few remarks about Bill C-47, which proposes to increase the capitalization of the Export Development Corporation, which is a Crown corporation. It seems to me that we went through this process not long ago. As a matter of fact we went through a very similar process-and quite a correct one-in 1974 when it was decided that EDC must come to parliament before making any changes in the total capitalization under which it operates. We went through this process when we considered Bill C-9, back in 1974, and here today we have an opportunity to make some observations with respect to Bill C-47.
Eventually this bill will get to committee, and the president of EDC will come before the committee and be questioned by hon. members of this House about the operation of that bank. It has been three years since members of parliament questioned officials of the bank and many serious questions have arisen not only about Canada's economic development but about our relationships with developing countries, especially our trade relationships.
We have witnessed the problems involving Argentina and Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. We know that EDC was involved in the lending of $129 million in that regard. We also witnessed the fiasco of EDC's lending money to International Nickel Company of Canada for its operation in Guatemala, a country in which a butcher is in power. His security is that of the armed forces. Yes, EDC lent INCO $28 million at prime rates of interest, at rates which we do not make available to Canadian low income earners in this country. I shall also deal later with some international ramifications. I shall speak of certain EDC operations and certain unpleasant relationships arising from Noranda moving into Chile.
It is good that the Canada Development Corporation, a Crown corporation, will be examined by a committee of this House. That examination will take place in the context of discussions on this bill, and once more we shall try to learn some answers, try to probe into the secrecy which shrouds the operations of this bank which the taxpayers of Canada supposedly own.
Export Development Act
For example, we still want to know what rates of interest are charged by EDC to countries with which we do business, and to corporations which borrow and whose loans are secured by EDC. We still want to know the basis, conditions and rationale on which such loans are made, and want to know if any international morality applies to the making of such loans. We want to know if any loans or relationships involve tied aid, that is to say, whether we tie loans to any conditions. Does the corporation lend money say, to Trinidad, or Guyana, or any other country, which must be used to purchase products in Canada? That sort of practice has been condemned universally, and we shall want to look into the corporation's operations to see if it is operating in this unfair and outmoded manner. First, then, we shall want to prod the secrecy under which the corporation operates.
The second thing we shall do, I suggest, is also important. One hears much talk in this House about the elimination of regional disparities. That concept has always struck me as being like motherhood. We all subscribe to it. I want to know if EDC operates with a complete lack of awareness of the objects of national development in this country? We have discovered, from previous discussions on similar bills involving EDC, that in 1973 the Export Development Corporation made loans amounting to $867.4 million in the Montreal area. In other words, 60.6 per cent of their total loans for that year were made in the Montreal area. Southern Ontario got $382.9 million, or 24.9 per cent of total loans in the area. Vancouver got $123.2 million, or 8.1 per cent; Calgary, $5.4 million, or 0.3 per cent; Atlantic Canada $90.4 million, or 5.9 per cent, and Winnipeg $.5 million, or 0.03 per cent. These figures are important.
It appears that here we have a Crown corporation lending money to stimulate industrial development in areas already heavily industrialized, while the government, under the DREE program, is supposedly trying to direct money to less well developed areas in order to further their development. It does not seem to make sense. We are spending millions upon millions of dollars through DREE and manpower retraining programs on areas which otherwise would have no chance of acquiring any kind of industrial development while, at the same time, we have another Crown corporation pouring millions of dollars into already heavily developed areas. This raises some important questions. Let me give some specific examples to show why I am concerned.
Consider the question of McKinnon Industries. They are going to build transmissions for a corporation operating in Venezuela. Obviously they obtained a loan. If they intend to expand their plant, they are not going to expand it in Sudbury. They are gong to expand where their plant is already located, in St. Catharines. In effect, therefore, Export Development Corporation, an agency of the government, is hiving off industrial development, as it were, from where it is needed. It is operating in complete ignorance of the government's objectives for industrial development. The government has enunciated its aims, and has attempted to carry them out by spending millions of dollars through the Department of Regional Eco-

April 27, 1977
Export Development Act
nomic Expansion and the RDIA program. This contradiction in aims boggles the mind. The corporation seems to act as if it is totally ignorant of the government's development aims.
It is important to consider something else, too, and the point may seem almost naive. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has talked to priests, ministers of the Cross, and Rabbis about morality, and suggested that the government ought to operate under some sort of moral sidelines. He suggested that we must show moral uprightness in our international relations if we are to expect our citizens to behave with decency and morality toward each other in society.
With this in mind, I come now to the clause to which I alluded earlier, and I raise again the involvement of EDC in that fiasco of a loan made in Argentina. I recall that this whole question was raised in the committee when it dealt with a somewhat similar bill to the one we are now discussing. We examined the president of EDC, Mr. Aitken, on how we lent money to Argentina with respect to the CAN DU reactor. This took place in November, 1974, at which time we raised the question of the government's rationale in rushing forward to sell the CANDU to Argentina as a loss leader, the government then knowing that Argentina had not signed the nonproliferation treaty concerning atomic weapons. We knew at that time that the Argentinian government was unstable, that it was in the hiatus of Isabella Perron's rule when murders were being committed almost every night and day. We knew there was the possibility of the military junta seizing power. That was imminent and real.
Despite all this, the government rushed in and lent Argentina $129 million for a CANDU reactor, I wish it were as willing to rush in and lend $129 million to the low income earners of this country. Such money would prevent them from going to loan sharks for money they need for necessities.
In the making of these loans I wish EDC would apply the same stringent criterion any bank applies to a small businessman seeking a loan. I wish it would ask questions like these: how stable is this operation? What is their collateral? What has been their past behaviour? Have they ever applied for a loan on previous occasions? But, no, they rush in, ready to lend. They made a $28 million loan to the International Nickel Company of Canada, to develop the lateritic ore in Guatemala. If ever there was a company powerful enough to generate its own capital by loans, it is International Nickel Company of Canada.
At that time Inco had laid off 5,000 workers in the Sudbury Basin over a period of two short years. But what did we find? We found the Export Development Corporation loaning $28 million to Inco to develop the lateritic ore. If the development of lateritic ore was to create jobs in Guatemala, I would be the first to say viva Guatemala. However, the number of jobs created by the lateritic ores, which are simply a scraping of ore off the ground, was absolutely minimal. All managerial positions in that operation were filled by strangers, not native Guatemalans.
We had a situation where force was needed by the butcher, to keep troops on guard to ensure the safety of the project in Guatemala. We moved in and aligned ourselves with the most disastrous and inhuman elements in the hemisphere when we started to lend money at premium rates to these corporations. I suggest that Inco was quite able to raise its own capital by going to the private or international banks and borrowing the money on their own hook.
We now have the spectacle of EDC rushing arm and arm with Noranda into Chile. If it were Nazi Germany today, I suspect the EDC would be the first one willing to go arm in arm with Hitler to develop an armaments factory as long as it meant a spin-off of a few shekels and jobs in the industrialized sector of Canada. That is absolutely distasteful.
At the United Nations we stood up and said that human rights had been violated in Chile under the military junta of Pinochet and company. We acquiesced in the Amnesty International report. It will be said that it was in the General Assembly and not in the Security Council. However, we were not on the Security Council until this year. In any event, we stood up in the United Nations and were counted. One would have hoped that some kind of indication of government morality was taking shape, yet here we have a government Crown corporation under the aegis of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien), and we cannot say they are innocent babes in the woods. They are knowledgeable, capable and willing partners in this brutalization of humanity in Chile. They are doing it willingly.
If the government had any kind of morality it would stay clear of that operation in Chile. That could be done through the United Nations until the situation is acceptable to Canadian participation in the development of that economy.
They can try using all the red herrings they want to alleviate the situation in Chile, but they are not doing that. All they are doing is shoving the people down further, and enhancing the junta. In fact General Pinochet said that although he would not be here forever, there would be no elections and that he would ensure there would be no elections after he is gone. I would expect the EDC to show some respect for the morality which this government and this country have shown in the United Nations and on other world stages.
Another question must be raised. This party is certainly not against assisting developing countries that are attempting to improve their economic position in the world and the economic and social well-being of their citizens. That is something we can support. However, we must be concerned about the kinds of loans that are made. Short-term loans and accumulating large amounts of outstanding debt over a short period of time place a great hardship on a developing country. It must spend more and more of its foreign reserves in order to pay the interest on the short-term large amounts of debt it has accumulated.
We want to look at the pattern of EDC lending since that corporation last appeared before a committee of this House. Indeed we want to see whether they have heeded the message of Vina del Mar. That was a special meeting at the ministerial

April 27, 1977

level of a special commission of Latin American countries in 1969. They reached one conclusion which ought to be of interest to people in the developed part of the world dealing with financing and investment. I quote the conclusion of this special ministerial conference at Vina del Mar:
"Inter-American financial co-operation ... should be a real transfer and be granted in accordance with national development policies and plans." Lenders "should base their co-operation on economic and social criteria," paying "particular attention ... to relatively less developed countries in the region. All stipulations and criteria which tie the use of loans to the acquisition of goods and services in given countries or from given sources should be abolished." Mechanisms are needed "to liberalize external credit, reduce interest rates and expand the volume and length of credits."
We want to know if the EDC is following the advice which the Latin American countries have given with respect to this whole question, namely, tying the loan to the purchase of equipment and services in the country issuing the loan. Members of this House ought to be concerned about how our Crown corporate banking institution operates in the world. It should be of grave concern to us at a time when we are paying lip service to the new international economic order. I am interested in knowing whether there has been any change in the philosophy of the Export Development Corporation with regard to the way it issues loans.
The last observation I want to make with regard to the EDC is one that was made the last time the EDC appeared before the committee. I want to get to the bottom of the way the corporation operates. It is essential that these Crown corporations be called before a committee of the House from time to time in order to review their thinking, the philosophy which motivates them, the manner in which they operate in order to ensure that it is in line with the acceptable practice of Canadians and the acceptable morality among Canadians at that time. We look forward to the committee stage of the bill and to being able to question officials of EDC, the minister, and other interested parties respecting the operations of this corporation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE THE MAXIMUM LIABILITY OF THE CORPORATION AND CREDIT GUARANTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief in this debate on Bill C-47, to amend the Export Development Act. My colleague from Regina East has outlined this party's position regarding the proposed amendments and the act itself; therefore, I will not dwell on the subject matter in general terms. Instead, I should like to make a few comments on the bill which deals, or rather omits to deal, with the area for which I am responsible on behalf of my party, that of small business.
All members of the House are aware of the over-all structure of the government's agencies. The Department of Supply and Services is responsible for the Canadian Export Corporation. CIDA falls under the Department of External Affairs, and of course the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce looks after the Export Development Corporation.
My concern, as well as the concern of thousands of small and medium sized enterprises across Canada, is that none of these three departments or their agencies has a policy, let
Export Development Act
alone a definition, regarding small and medium enterprises, a sector which is responsible for the employment of the majority of the labour force in Canada today and which is sadly being bypassed in the formation of legislative programs such as this.
It is fine for the amendment before us to increase the maximum liability of the Export Development Corporation under contracts of insurance entered into and guarantees issued under the provisions referred to in the amended section from $750 million to $2,500 million. No one has any concern about that aspect of the bill. Unfortunately this does not in any way extend the opportunities of the largest sector of our economy to get involved in the export development business with EDC or any other government agency.
A sector which in many cases is competitive in nature and tops in potential employment opportunities-a very important fact to keep in mind is that small and medium size business enterprises in Canada are definitely potentially the most economic employment opportunity in our economy-is suppressed time and again by government bureaucracy on the one hand and by lack of positive incentive programs on the other. I realize that the Small Business Loans Act was introduced for second reading just last Friday, and I look forward to taking part in the debate on that measure as well. I will not dwell on it except to say it seems very strange to us on this side of the House that, every time some semblance of improvement within the small business community appears to be likely through the legislative process of this House, we find it is based on recommendations which this party has been making for years. We do not want thanks from the government, but the least the government could do is to make the public aware of the fact that some of the recommendations did indeed come from this party.
It is unfortunate that there does not exist in the act or in this amendment a condition in the guarantee which would include a reasonable portion of the guarantee to be subcontracted to small and medium size industries in Canada. In contrast, for example, the United States Congress has declared a policy which outlines various areas of support to small business. Their policy, of course, begins with a definition. In Canada we do not have this. As a matter of fact the Minister of State (Small Businesses) (Mr. Marchand) does not even have the semblance of an idea about a definition of small and medium size enterprises, and I do not believe it is his intention to establish one. Therefore how can a government, with no definition of this vital sector of our economy, be expected to establish a policy within that sector?

speechtext:
It is just a political gesture, my colleague says. The situation is different in the United States where in 1975 alone $18 billion worth of contracts out of a total of $54 billion went to small business for U.S. government purchases of goods and services. There is a definition of "small business" in the United States; an owner managed enterprise which is not dominant in the field is their definition. It is the working definition of every department of industry or agency connected

April 27, 1977
Export Development Act
therewith in the United States; therefore policies are based on that definition. In Canada the small businessman is barely scraping the bottom of the barrel when it comes to a definition, or what are known as set aside programs.
By not having multinational companies subcontracting to small business, the EDC is simply trying to make an obsolete model workable. It is not beneficial to our balance of payments and certainly not to our unemployment problems to allow the EDC to help a mere 20 or 25 multinationals instead of acting on a broader basis. It is true that the EDC's mandate is to assist those corporations incorporated in Canada. It is also true, however, that the same mandate does not specify Canadian ownership. For example, the diesel division of General Motors of Canada has made sales of locomotives to Egypt to the tune of $7.6 million. That is fine, but do they need assistance from the EDC? Would a Canadian owned company get this kind of assistance? The Douglas Aircraft Company, another U.S. owned enterprise, has had assistance from government agencies to sell $1.2 million worth of components alone to Brazil. I should not even mention the $250 million CANDU reactor sales to Korea, Mr. Speaker.
To limit the guarantees to such large, foreign owned multinationals only is not going to help this country's economy in the long run. We must instead follow the examples set in the United States, Japan, West Germany and elsewhere. We do not have to be embarrassed by following some workable examples which have been established in other countries. Sometimes when these recommendations are made we are criticized for following in the footsteps of other industrialized nations, but surely there is nothing wrong in following in the footsteps of successful industrialized nations or adopting the successful programs of those nations.
Conditions for the EDC granting export credits to large firms only with the understanding that a fair proportion of subcontracts be given to small and medium sized industries must be considered, so that we can get a broader range of interest, a broader range of assistance and a broader understanding of the problems of the export market in Canada, as a result of which small businessmen from coast to coast who cannot export on their own will be given assistance, rather than such assistance going to large multinational corporations which can export on their own. This is the unfair portion of this over-all program. We must, at the same time, consider charging the same interest rates to big business as the FBDB charges to small business. We will get into this when the Small Businesses Loans Act comes before this House, for obvious reasons. It is my belief that only then, when this program is broadened to include the bulk of the enterprises in Canada rather than the few large ones, will the largest deficit of balance of payments per capita in the world that we in Canada have today be somewhat altered. We must include the grass roots level of the industrial complex of Canada.
At the outset I said I would be brief. Therefore I will close by saying that I look forward to discussing this bill in commit-

tee stage, at which time I hope to make my specific recommendations in this regard, perhaps in the form of amendments.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE THE MAXIMUM LIABILITY OF THE CORPORATION AND CREDIT GUARANTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, along with others who have already spoken I do not plan to take a great deal of the time of the House on this particular measure. It is generally agreed that if the government had, in the first instance, introduced this matter as a legislative proposal, we would have had it out of the way long before this.
I do want to speak to two things with respect to the responsibilities of the Export Development Corporation, both as they affect the Canadian economy and also as they affect our international relationships, and particularly the situation with developing countries. It is interesting to realize in the breakdown of expenditures, as mentioned by the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), that something less than 1 per cent of the finances of the Export Development Corporation are, in a sense, dispersed throughout the Atlantic region. When you put that 1 per cent figure against the rough population figure of 10 per cent, you realize what kind of discrimination does exist with respect to this particular federal program.
In spite of some of the rhetoric that has been used recently by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) or his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), I do not think we should be fooled by the fact that time and again throughout various government departments, agencies and Crown corporations, we see policies in effect that work against the so-called commitment to eradicate our substantial regional disparities. That is the obvious lesson we must learn from the economic attempts over the past 15 years.
While we have established numerous programs like ARDA, FRED, comprehensive development plans and, more recently, local initiatives, Canada Works, Atlantic development boards, and even adjustment grants of one kind or another, very often these direct programs are not only undercut but the impact of them is substantially destroyed by the continuing activity in tens of areas of government programs and policies that provide their own kind of regional program, but a regional program in reverse. It is a program of creating even greater economic activity and benefit in the highly developed regions of the country, and substantially reducing or taking away from those areas which are already greatly dependent and under-utilized.
The symbolic fact, when we look at the location of offices of the Export Development Corporation, with offices in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver, is we realize that there is not even an office in any of the four Atlantic provinces. I suppose the argument will be made, when we have a chance to discuss this with members of the corporation when they come before committee, that naturally with such a small amount of business-something less than 1 per cent-it would be highly impractical and extremely expensive for them to locate an office anywhere in the Atlantic region. This is the vicious circle with which we are faced.
On the one hand a corporation such as the Export Development Corporation says that there is not enough business in the
April 27, 1977

Atlantic provinces, therefore we do not have an office. On the other hand, if there is no one in the area to attempt to develop possible trading and possible export advantages in the region, there is no earthly way that the particular business and industrial ventures in Atlantic Canada are ever going to make use of that opportunity. Until we realize that fact, we have to recognize there is no serious, pervasive, and comprehensive approach to dealing with regional and economic social disparity.
As long as we have most of our efforts under one or two departments such as the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the Department of Manpower and Immigration, and still have 20 or more other departments, not to mention the fact that there are hundreds of Crown corporations and agencies that have no criteria and have no priorities with respect to the regional, economic and social development of the country, we are just going to be playing games.
We are not seriously committing the total impact of federal government policies to dealing on a long term and continuing basis with the reduction of regional disparities. I say that clearly today because I hope when the corporation officials come before our committee they will be able to explain the mandate they have been given or the instructions under which they operate whereby they take into account the situation of economic opportunities and the export opportunities that may exist in the regional disadvantaged areas. If they are unable to explain that, if they have given little or no thought to it and have received no instruction on it from the federal government, one must assume that this is just one more indication that there is no comprehensive approach on the part of the government. I wanted to say that clearly at this point on the second reading of the bill.
The prime purpose of the Export Development Corporation is to assist Canadian enterprises to achieve sales and to maximize their export opportunities abroad. I want to look at the basis on which such decisions are taken. As I read in the annual report for 1976, there is a statement early on which sets the framework for the purpose on which the Export Development Corporation operates. I will not repeat all of it. It is found on pages 11 and 12 of the document. On page 12, particularly, it reads:
The export transaction must maximize significant benefits to Canada and must withstand a detailed review of the relative merits of the proposal.
The first part, the maximizing of significant benefits to Canada, is obvious. What is not so obvious, as I said a moment ago, is that it is not maximizing benefits equally and fairly to the whole of Canada. As has already been pointed out this afternoon, the benefits are not equal. They are tending to create a further imbalance in our economy. 1 think it is something about which we should be very concerned.
The second thing I would like to say is that it does not clearly state what kinds of benefits, if any, should be taken into account in dealing in transactions with the countries which are the recipients in this case. Those are the countries that are usually listed as the borrowers in this instance. There are a number of borrowers, as one would expect, for a country like
Export Development Act
Canada which is a major trading nation. While we have a list published in this annual report of a variety of endeavours and activities in many countries, the only thing we are told is a very general comment on the nature of the activity, the amount of money involved, and something about the repayment terms.
The countries are quite a mixed group. I am certainly not going to try to deal with all the countries named in this particular report, but there are some that concern me very much. I am referring to countries like Argentina, Brazil, Indonesia and South Africa. These countries all have one thing very clearly in common. They have come increasingly under condemnation for their excessive and continuing violation of human rights.
It is interesting to note over the past few months that the subject of human rights and economic assistance have become major topics. If I were to even raise the question in this debate, or if I had raised it a few months ago, people would have regarded it as a naive and irrelevant question to put to members of this House. But since it has become the focus of a good deal of attention over the past two of three years in the U.S. Congress, at the United Nations, and most recently in the enunciations of President Carter, it is not far removed from our concerns, or it should not be. If the officers and staff of the Export Development Corporation think that this is beyond their mandate or beyond their consideration, I trust they will begin to give it very serious consideration. I say that because in most of the major economic institutions that operate on an international basis today there is a fundamental re-examination of the relationship between various forms of economic assistance and activity and the impact of those programs on the human rights of people who live in the recipient countries.
Let me quote from the testimony of a witness who appeared before the subcommittee on international development yesterday, Mr. Earl Drake, the Canadian Executive Director of the World Bank. He appeared before our committee to discuss the whole question of international debt. At one point during the hearing, my hon. friend, the member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather), asked him whether other aspects aside from basic or limited economic questions were taken into account when determining the activities of the World Bank and the loans which it made. Here is part of the answer Mr. Drake gave yesterday morning:
But when it comes to human rights, I am a bit ambivalent on this because in the very broadest definition of human rights, that is really what we are involved in in the World Bank. We are trying to help the human condition of mankind. There are human rights involving, I think, a decent standard of living and that is what we are trying to improve.
We are trying to make it possible for every man to grow up in decency with minimum conditions of health and education and opportunity for employment. And 1 have to admit to you that I think that a political atmosphere in which people are free to express their opinions, free from arbitrary imprisonment or torture is related to that. As an individual I have to concede that. But I have ... It is difficult for the bankers and institutions to come to grips with it because we are not human rights experts, we do not have the data, we are an institution which lives on data. We feed in material all the time, we try to be objective, we

April 27, 1977
Export Development Act
try to quantify everything we deal with. And we are not equipped to deal with it. We do not have the expertise, we do not have the data.
My own feeling on this is that if some other body, some United Nations body, could make judgments on human rights, could make a finding that some countries are so derelict in their respective human rights that they deserve to be outside the pale, that it is not possible to carry on a dialogue about the betterment of economic conditions because basic conditions are not there, if they would make that judgment then I think that the World Bank as a member body of the United Nations should take that into account and that our articles should be changed to do it. But I do think it is wrong for any one country to try to impose its standards.
This raises one or two questions which obviously I shall not have time to explore. It does call attention to the fact that our senior director on the board of the World Bank has realized that there is a basic question of human rights involved here, and one which can no longer be ignored.
It is not possible, or perhaps it would not be very effective, for individual countries to make determinations solely on the basis of a subjective or political approach, but if we could create some international machinery, for example, if an agency of the United Nations were to consider this question, the judgment of such a body would have some influence in a determination of the justification for economic assistance or loans. These are considerations of the kind which are very much front and centre in the United States Congress today. They reflect the position taken by President Carter recently with respect to three countries, Argentina, Uruguay, and Ethiopia and, if I may say so, they are very much the concerns of a bill which I introduced about a month ago, Bill C-404, which would give the Canadian government the authority to make decisions with regard to economic assistance based on the judgment of the International Commission of Jurists, a body which has experience in this field and is accredited by the United Nations.
As the directors and staff of the Export Development Corporation well know, there has been increasing criticism recently from a variety of sources, particularly from church and humanitarian groups, with respect to major loans which have been made, or which are contemplated, by the Export Development Corporation to countries grossly and continuously violating basic human rights. Perhaps the most celebrated and the most current of these considerations relate to the financing of export assistance to the Noranda Corporation and the development of the copper mining operation in Chile. I suppose it is of concern because here is the commitment of a Canadian Crown corporation through a private Canadian company to invest a significant amount of funds in a major copper mining industry in Chile, in a country which we are painfully aware has done some unbelievable and terrible things to its own citizens in terms of imprisonment, arrest, assassinations, torture and expulsion and intimidation.
I am sure that many Canadians have wondered at the Justification for the use of Canadian funds, both public and private, being extended to a military machine which, in a continuing way, violates the human rights of its own citizens. I am not saying here, Mr. Speaker, anything half as strong as has been reported in various United Nations findings and raised repeatedly in committees of the United Nations. I do

not need to remind hon. members that it was two other members of parliament along with myself who, on the eve of a visit to Chile in order to investigate the substance of continuing criticism of that country from the human rights point of view, were refused entry.
I know that the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury), who is chairman of Interparliamentary Union, attempted, along with his hon. friends, to persuade the Chilean authorities to allow independent fact finding with regard to the situation and, in particular, to make inquiries concerning a number of former parliamentarians who have been imprisoned, apparently without due cause-some of them have been tortured and otherwise harassed.
I bring all this before the House today because when we are dealing with agencies which operate on behalf of the people of Canada we must be sure there is no possibility that the economic benefits which will be provided will not encourage a continuance of repression or oppression in countries which have become notorious internationally for systematic violations of human rights. It is not really necessary to say anything about the situation in Chile because it has been so extensively documented and recorded over the past few years. Increasingly questions have been raised about countries such as Argentina and Uruguay. These are two countries which we had the opportunity to visit last fall. From our own experience of interviewing refugees, former prisoners and others who had been ill-treated or intimidated, we know only too well the level to which respect for human rights in Argentina has fallen. In Uruguay the situation is even more depressing. Nor do conditions in Brazil offer any encouragement to those concerned about the basic civil liberties which we cherish so highly in this country. Thus, when the Export Development Corporation says in its report that it must "maximize benefits to Canada and withstand a detailed review of each proposal" one still hopes there will be a good deal more forthcoming in the future than in the past.
Certainly attempts by interested parties to find out in a responsible way what way the Export Development Corporation is taking all factors into account with respect to its programs, its loans and its insurance policies, should be clearly answered. There can be no justification in this day and age for this secrecy.
I know that in the world of corporate business there is always a concern that in certain areas a business enterprise may be jeopardized because a certain amount of its business information may become public and therefore available in some kind of advantageous way to its competitors. However, I certainly believe that in this day and age we have enough sophistication and understanding of the way in which business operates that the information that is required in order to ease the mind and to justify the transactions of the corporation can be clearly made available to the Canadian people. I hope that we will have the opportunity, when this matter comes to committee, to hear the chairman of the corporation and his
April 27, 1977

officials state clearly what are the factors that have been taken into account, and what is the present and detailed relationship with respect to investments in countries such as Chile, Argentina, Brazil, and Indonesia.
As a matter of fact I find it passing strange that the corporation could not make that kind of basic explanation to the Canadian people on why it should ask for the considerable increase in insurability that it is looking for in this legislation or in future legislation which, I understand, is to follow, because it seems to me that if a corporation of this nature cannot make its case to the Canadian people, it has no right to exist as a corporation on their behalf, as is presently the case. Therefore, without adding many more words at this time, let me say that I look forward to having further detailed discussions when this measure comes to committee.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to add a few words to this debate with respect to Bill C-47. As has already been pointed out, it is a rather simple amendment to the existing legislation with respect to the Export Development Corporation, but I think there are some points that should be made abundantly clear for the record.
The first point is that the bill before us is the result of an objection taken mainly by this party to a procedure whereby the minister attempted to slip through the legislation we have now before us as a $1 item in the estimates of his department. In short, if the minister had been allowed to slip that $1 item through, parliament would have been denied the right to review the legislation we have before us and to have members of the Export Development Corporation staff appear before the appropriate committee to explain why they felt that the legislation should be amended.
When you think that we are dealing in terms of approximately $2 billion in additional authorized liability of the Export Development Corporation with respect to insurance activities, it is staggering that the minister would have even tried to slip this through committee simply with a $1 item during consideration of estimates.
Having said that, I make it clear that we believe that the insurance side of the Export Development Corporation activities is the more credible side of what the corporation is doing. I say that because, if you assess the insurance activities of EDC, most people would agree that generally the corporation is dealing with a relatively small customer, their diversification is credible, and their ratios, so far as claims are concerned, are not out of line. On the other hand, when we take a look at EDC financing and loan activities, that is where I believe the House must pay close attention. The fact is that EDC, with respect to a select few customers-and unfortunately the corporation is maintaining that approach-is extending hundreds of millions of dollars of credit that we will have to write off at some future date, and unfortunately this will be done with recourse to no one.
The annual report that we have before us points out the magnitude of some of these write-offs that are starting to develop. I would refer hon. members to page 42 of the report
Export Development Act
which has been signed by the Auditor General of Canada as of March 23. For example, this report was denied us at the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs when there was an attempt to slip the $1 item through. We were denied the up-to-date figures on how EDC was doing. But the reason I refer hon. members to this report at page 42 is that it is very interesting to read the Auditor General's report on loans receivable. He points out that the aggregate loans receivable as of the end of December amount to $1,343 million. He then states:
The future economic and political conditions in some of the countries where the corporation has made loans are unpredictable and accordingly possible losses to the corporation are not susceptible to accurate measurement. During the year ended December 31, 1976, a provision for loss in the amount of $2,000,000 has been made, and an amount of $8,000,000 of retained earnings has been appropriated to the reserve for underwriting and lending contingencies.
But then, most significantly, he states:
During 1976, the corporation rescheduled payments due of $13,683,000. These reschedulings are intended to aid collectibility and servicing of the debt. Since inception of the export loans program in 1961, the corporation has rescheduled $61,196,000, none of which is overdue at December 31, 1976.
At December 31, 1976, $2,458,000 of accrued interest is overdue.
The reason 1 read that into the record is that in plain language, getting away from the fancy wording of an auditor, we are already in default with respect to some of our foreign lending activities to the tune of $61 million. That is the amount that various borrowers around the world have found it difficult to repay on schedule to us, and the classic way of covering up the mistakes is to reschedule, as they say.
It is like going to your bank where you have borrowed some money and, instead of repaying your loan, you ask the bank manager to give you extended terms, and somehow you paper the thing over to make it appear that you are no longer in default. That was exactly the problem of Atlantic Acceptance. That was the game that was played at that time with respect to defaulting creditors. The president of Atlantic Acceptance Finance always pretended that his loans were paid off on time. What he systematically did a few weeks before the year's end was to have his managers call in all of his creditors and simply re-issue new notes, apparently giving them a current status. That is what EDC is starting to do with respect to its $1,343 million in loans to foreign countries. That is what we are alarmed about and that is what the government should be alarmed about, but the minister appears to be totally indifferent to what EDC is doing. Perhaps it is beyong his grasp.
Having said that, I would like to emphasize, however, that that is the financing side of EDC. That is where EDC is likely to get into trouble. For example, the previous president of EDC admitted that if EDC attempted to liquidate the loans it has on its books, the loss, to use his words, would be infinite. In truth, EDC does not have loans which would have any marketable value in relation to their face value, and we are basically getting into a very awkward situation where we are going to find that year by year more and more of these loans are going to have to be rescheduled, and they may never be collected

What I am saying is that the insurance side has always facilitated the relatively small deal in a much more effective way than has the lending side, and unfortunately, not only has the lending side chosen to deal with relatively large amounts, but it also deals with a very select few party faithful companies, which tend to get well over 50 per cent of the total lending of EDC. We know how the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) has been protective with respect to the appointment of commissioners to take a census. Mr. Speaker, it was obvious, once the new year had come in and the government had failed to refer the white paper on the Bank Act revisions to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, that we were in deep trouble with regard to processing both the white paper and any legislation in time for the July 1, 1977, expiry date of the present Bank Act. There is nothing to indicate that the problems which the government may have to face with regard to some of the provisions and proposals in the white paper have been solved.
At this time it is not my intention to get into the subject of banking or agreement as to the provisions of this bill. It is not my intention to discuss them at all. It is simply a question of determining what will be the date of extension. For some people it appears that there is something strange about extending the date of the Bank Act or that its life should be extended. That is because most hon. members are not aware that in the mid-1960's we extended the life of the Bank Act twice, each time by a whole year. In fact it went from 1964, which was the normal expiry date, to July 1, 1966. There was a salutary period of three months or so after passage of the act before it came into force because certain steps had to be taken by some banks as a result of the changes. That is why we are looking at a date.
I hope I can convince the government that the proposals contained in clause 6 of this bill are not the right ones. There should be a fixed date. Who can forecast whether parliament will sit at least 20 days during the month of December, 1977? However, there is nothing saying that parliament cannot sit for 20 days in December. The act would not come into force until the sixtieth sitting day of parliament next thereafter. That, in itself, is terribly uncertain.
