Mr. Speaker, I am glad that such a high level of agreement exists in the House today. I share that. I am almost willing to agree to anything these days just to see some legislation get through the House. It would make me feel a little better about the salary I get.
While parliament has never been known for its speed, and it has never been a Speedy Gonzales, the present pace at which legislation is getting through the House makes a snail look like a candidate for a speeding ticket. In my view there has never been so much legislation come in, go back, be referred back, and come back to the House. It seems almost impossible to get anything through these days. I do not know the problem. We are consulting ourselves and carrying the business of going back and forth with legislation to the point where rigor mortis has almost set in in terms of the Order Paper and what is going through.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) is concerned about setting a date rather than the formula which the government is proposing. He should not be terribly concerned about that. The way we are going, the Bank Act will not be passed before the next election. In fact we may not see much else in the way of legislation passed before the next election. I do not know whether it is the slowness of the government, or deliberate on the part of the government that they picked up so much of the Tory philosophy that they figure the least done is the best done.
There does not seem to be any real indication that legislation is going to go through this House to any extent. The fault has to be the government's. The government can argue as much as it likes about the opposition not co-operating. There is some truth to that argument, but the opposition is not known for its co-operativeness under the best of circumstances.
The government has all the instruments at its disposal for ensuring that legislation goes through the House. It has the power to act, but it has not acted. It is as though it does not want to act. The government does not care whether the Bank Act or anything else goes through in this session. I guess it is on the theory that if you do not do anything, nobody can fault you.
Consider how many times the Borrowers and Lenders Act has been in and out. In the case of budgets, often we are still

debating a budget at the time we are asking the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) when he is going to introduce a new budget. One seems to follow on the other until you get so confused that you do not know whether what you are talking about was in the old budget or in the new budget.
Recently the Unemployment Insurance Act was being changed. The gun control laws are being changed. The consumers act has been in and out. The hon. member for Edmonton West the other day, in a very excellent and lively speech, said that you almost have to do a strip-tease to get any recognition from this House. The hon. member doing a striptease would be a welcome respite from some of the things that have been going on in this House. Therefore I would like to see this matter dealt with now. I do not think we have any choice.
The Bank Act should have been passed a long time ago. I do not agree with the hon. member for Edmonton West that it does not make any difference. There is a tremendous amount of difference in some of the proposals that are in the white paper on the Bank Act. It will significantly affect banking and competition in this country. We should be moving in that direction, or at least finding out what will be the future shape of banking in Canada.
The consequence of these pieces of legislation hanging around is that a political and economic vacuum is created. Nobody knows the rules of the game. People cannot make any decisions about the future and what their role in that future will be. I do not agree it does not make any difference if it takes a little longer or hangs around for a little while. It is of critical importance that so little is being done in the way of legislation. This kind of mushball approach to getting things done points out an absence of planning. The government does not know what it is doing. It tends to respond to whoever yells the loudest or puts on the most pressure at any given time.
I do not want to contribute unduly to delaying this legislation even though it is only legislation not to do anything. That is what it amounts to, Mr. Speaker. However, even this will show up somewhere as something that we have passed in this parliament, and I think we should get on with it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words at this stage of Bill C-39 extending the Bank Act and the Quebec Savings Banks Act. Even if I have been sitting in this House for some 15 years already, I am always surprised to see the planning that goes into the government's work. It is always late, it is always down to the last minute when it comes to legislation like this. For example, when we had to pass the last Bank Act renewing the banks charter in 1967, the government knew then that that act was effective for only 10 years. It is unforgivable that the government should have waited until March 7, 1977 to introduce a bill which had to be passed for July 1, 1977. Obviously that time was much too short. The government should have better planned its work and introduced that bill a lot earlier so the House would have time to consider the bill and amend the Bank Act so it would take effect on July 1, 1977.
April 27, 1977

So we are caught short and asked to extend the Bank Act until at least January 1, 1978, but a provision in Bill C-39 says that if the House of Commons does not sit 20 days in December 1977 the banks will be able to continue their operations under the present system until the 60th sitting day of the House in 1978.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have checked and there are only 15 days in December on which the House can sit, unless it decides to sit between Christmas and New Year's which, I believe, has never happened in the past. It is obvious that the government wants to extend the Bank Act to late in 1978. I, for one, have no objection in this regard because for several decades, every-time we have renewed the bank charter, banks have always obtained very important concessions. I think that banks are not to be pitied now. They make substantial profits and there is nothing urgent about amending the Bank Act to grant them further concessions on top of those they already enjoy.
Mr. Speaker, 1 have one criticism to make, regarding the planning of the business of the House which, whenever deadlines such as these are imposed, does not bring forward legislation early enough to enable hon. members to give it proper consideration so that it can be passed in time. Therefore, 1 have no objection to consider this bill at this stage this afternoon, in committee of the whole so that it can be passed immediately. It is not time, I suggest, to consider the principle of the Bank Act. We will have the opportunity of doing so when the act itself is introduced, and we reserve the right to do it at that time through a clause by clause examination.
Mr. Speaker, I think we should consider the bill in committee of the whole and pass it at all stages today, up to third reading.

Mr. Speaker, my first intervention on this matter was in the nature of a point of order. I should like the opportunity to say a few words about the bill, which amends section 6 of the Bank Act and of the Quebec Savings Banks Act to permit the banks chartered under those acts to carry on business until January 1, 1978. This short bill is necessary because it is now evident that it will not be possible to introduce and to have passed by parliament before July 1 the government's decennial revision proposals for the Bank Act and related legislation.
The development and the drafting of this legislation is taking longer than was originally envisaged. I might inform the House, in view of some criticisms which have been made of the government, that the delays are not owing to any conservatism on the part of the government or to any feeling that the Bank Act revisions should not be undertaken; it is simply due to extra pressure of work which has fallen on the particular officials who have been engaged in and are responsible for the drafting of this particular type of legislation.
Not only was there the budget, which has just been completed, but also there was the recent fiscal arrangements act
Bank Act
which hon. members will recall was one of the most complicated pieces of legislation ever dealt with by this parliament and which took an enormous amount of effort and time on the part of the most skilled members of the Department of Justice and Department of Finance to draft on behalf of the government.
The extension of the existing act has many precedents. In the first half of this century the act was similarly extended three times, in 1911, 1912 and 1933, and in the period from June, 1964, to July, 1967, it was extended five times. The delay at that time was in part to receive the report of the royal commission on banking and finance and to give the public and the government time to digest its recommendations.
On this occasion the decennial process is taking longer than was originally envisaged, for three reasons: firstly, the extent of consultations encouraged by the issuance of a white paper; secondly, the size and complexity of the task; and thirdly, the extent of other pressures on the small group of legislative drafters in the Department of Justice.
This bill will extend the decennial revision by approximately six months and will look again at the time limits, as I suggested earlier when the bill moves to committee stage. The intention in introducing it is to help ensure that by this extension parliament will have ample time, after the introduction of the decennial revision legislation some time before the summer recess, to give the legislation the time and attention it deserves.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BUSINESS PERIOD OF BANKS UNDER JURISDICTION OF QUEBEC SAVINGS BANKS ACT AND BANK ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman), has already indicated, we are quite prepared to agree to this extention of time for the Bank Act. However, I hope I will be pardoned if 1 indulge in a moment of historical reflection which leads me to the conclusion that somewhere along the line we are going to lose a decade.
I remember when I first came here that we knew that the Bank Act of 1934 would run out in 1944. The government of that day asserted that it was not going to ask for an extension, as the Bennett government had done in 1933, and that the act would be passed in 1944. Well, Mr. Speaker, it was. Next year is 1978, and so in three decades we will have lost four years. That leads me to suggest that before my days in this place are over we may well have lost a full decade. It begins to make a mockery of the idea that there is something sacred about this ten year life that we give to the chartered banks.
I appreciate the problems the government side has, and I appreciate the fact that the act has been extended before in 1911, 1912, and 1933, and at other times during the last three or four decades. But I hope some day we might move the other way and not lose a decade out of Canadian bank history.
Motion as amended agreed to, bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Laniel in the chair.
